title: Thinking Before You Act
note: How a ruler examines each task before he does it. Once the great have become useful helpers he does this with them, so it follows the chapter on petty company.

couplets.plain: Weigh what will be lost, what will be gained, and the profit it will bring later, then act.
couplets.pm: Weigh what the work will cost now, what will come back after that loss, and the profit it will bring later, and act if it is worthwhile. Worthwhile means that the return now exceeds the loss and keeps growing later. If that later profit is there, the work shouldn’t be dropped even when loss and return are equal now. See gain at both times, then act.

links.quote: Weigh what will be lost, what will be gained
the profit it will bring later, then act
links.reason: Gives anyone planning a venture the first job: weigh loss, gain and later profit.

couplets.plain: For those who examine a task with people they have chosen, think it over and then act, nothing is out of reach.
couplets.pm: For rulers who examine a fit task with the group they have chosen, then think it over themselves and can carry it through, nothing is hard to obtain. The task means everything from marching out to victory. Since they don’t fail in what is the source of wealth, all rare things come to them easily.

links.quote: examine a task with people they have chosen

links.remove: The ruler is his reading and the old English’s. The Tamil says only those who act.

couplets.plain: The wise won’t start a venture that looks for profit and loses the capital.
couplets.pm: The wise won’t take up work that, for the sake of future profit, may lose even the capital they already hold. Such work is like setting out to seize another’s land, without knowing your strength, the time or the place, and losing your own. This holds even for work already begun.

links.quote: The wise won’t start a venture
looks for profit and loses the capital

couplets.plain: Those who fear the stain of disgrace won’t begin what they are not sure of.
couplets.pm: Those who fear the fault of disgrace won’t start work they haven’t examined and settled, with their group and alone. Once begun, it can’t be dropped halfway. Disgrace is the scorn the world adds when the work fails, saying they have neither sense nor honour. That scorn is certain, so begin only where you are clear.

links.quote: won’t begin what they are not sure of

couplets.plain: To march out without thinking through every side of it is a way of planting your enemies in a prepared bed.
couplets.pm: For a ruler to march on his enemies having weighed only some of what may happen is a way of settling them in ground where they will grow. All of it means the position of both sides in strength, time and place, how to begin, the obstacles and how to clear them, how to win, and what is gained. Leave any of it out and the enemy has an opening.

links.quote: without thinking through every side of it
planting your enemies in a prepared bed

couplets.plain: You are ruined by doing what should not be done. You are ruined too by not doing what should.
couplets.pm: A ruler is ruined by doing what he should not, and ruined as well by not doing what he should. What he should not do is work that takes great effort, that gives little or no result, that is uncertain, or that brings sorrow later. What he should do is the reverse. Either error shrinks his wealth and army, so his enemies find him easy.

couplets.plain: Think, then commit to the task. To say you will think after you have committed is a mistake.
couplets.pm: Even when a task is fit to do, think out the means of finishing it before you start, because saying you will start now and think later is a fault. The means are four: gifts, sweet words, division and punishment. Start without thinking these through and the enemy blocks the work, it can’t be dropped halfway, and the ruler suffers.

links.quote: Think, then commit to the task

couplets.plain: Effort not made the right way will crack, though many stand by to guard it.
couplets.pm: Effort without the means that work will go wrong, though many helpers stand guard. It brings harm you didn’t intend instead of the good you did. The right means are gifts for the greedy, sweet words for the upright, the lazy and the battle-worn, division for those with allies or at odds with their own side, and force where these fail and on base men who can’t be trusted.

links.quote: Effort not made the right way will crack

couplets.plain: Even doing good can go wrong, if you don’t do it knowing each person’s nature.
couplets.pm: Even using the good means on other rulers can fail, unless you study each one’s character and act to suit it. The good means are gifts and sweet words, which are pleasant to everyone. Not suiting them means using them on those they aren’t fit for. Going wrong means the task isn’t finished.
couplets.note: He takes நன்று as gifts and sweet words used on other rulers, not as kindness in general.

links.quote: Even doing good can go wrong

couplets.plain: Think first, and do what no one will scorn. The world won’t accept what doesn’t suit you.
couplets.pm: If rulers, to finish a task, use means that don’t suit their position, the world scorns them, so they should seek means it won’t scorn. Not suiting means a strong ruler using gifts and the two other means fit for the weak, or a weak ruler using force, which is fit for the strong. Only fools do these. Match the means to your own strength or weakness.

links.quote: do what no one will scorn
links.reason: The world scorns what doesn’t suit you, so choose only what no one will scorn.
